items.title: On the line
items.text:
Sample text to test the reading width. The morning was flat and grey, the kind of calm that makes the water look like poured metal, and I sat on the edge of the boat for a long time before getting in. There is a moment before every dive where the body argues with the plan, and I have learned to let it talk without answering.

The rope hangs straight down into blue that gets darker without ever becoming black. You follow it with your hands, not your eyes. Somewhere around ten metres the sound changes; the boat engine and the voices above fall away and what is left is the click of your own ears equalizing and a pressure that feels less like weight and more like being held.

I used to think the hard part was going down. It turns out the hard part is staying still while everything in you wants to hurry. Hurrying costs oxygen. Thinking costs oxygen. Even wanting costs oxygen. So you practise wanting less, at least for forty seconds at a time.

On the way back up the light comes first as a rumour and then all at once. You break the surface and the air is loud and bright and ordinary, and for a few minutes everything on land seems slightly too fast. I write this down so I remember that the slowness was real, that it was there under the water the whole time, and that I can go back to it.

Later, drying off on the deck, someone asked what I think about down there. Nothing, I said, which was almost true. Mostly I count. Mostly I listen. Mostly I wait for the rope to tell me it is time to turn around.
